tip: Χαραγμένη (kharaghméni = etched) opens the sentence: the -μένος (-ménos) ending names a lasting state, not an action.
A past story can run in the present tense for vividness: μπαίνει... καταλαβαίνει (béni... katalavéni = he walks in... he realises).
Μολονότι (molonóti) is the formal 'although'; everyday Greek says αν και (an ke). Same meaning, but writing and literature prefer the heavier word.
The -ώμενη (-ómeni) ending is the bookish way to say 'while doing': αναρωτώμενη (anarotómeni) = wondering, as she watched the landscape.
Greek often reports a thought with no quotation marks: δεν θα του το πω (dhen tha tu to po = I won't tell him), σκέφτηκε (skéftike = she thought).
-οντας (-óndas) is the everyday 'while doing' ending: φτάνοντας στο λιμάνι (ftánondas sto limáni = arriving at the harbour) sets the scene.
Σαν να (san na) = as if; the verb after it keeps the tense of the story: σαν να φοβόταν (san na fovótan = as if she was afraid).
Αφήνω (afíno) + να (na) = let someone do something: άφησε τα βήματά του να τον οδηγήσουν (áfise ta vímatá tu na ton odhiyísun = he let his steps lead him).
Doubling καλά (kalá = well) turns it into 'even properly': πριν καλά καλά ξημερώσει (prin kalá kalá ksimerósi) = before day had even broken.
Όμως (ómos = but) moves around: it can open the clause – όμως εκείνος ήξερε (ómos ekínos íksere = but he knew) – or come second: εκείνος όμως (ekínos ómos).
The -μένος (-ménos) ending describes a state someone is in, not an action: αναγεννημένος (anayeniménos = reborn, renewed).
The ongoing past form paints a scene that keeps going: η βροχή χτυπούσε (i vrokhí khtipúse = the rain was beating, all night long).
For 'had done', Greek uses είχε (íkhe = had) plus one fixed verb form: είχε ήδη αποφασίσει (íkhe ídhi apofasísi = had already decided). Αποφασίσει stays the same for every person.
Λες και (les ke) = as if, the everyday twin of σαν να (san na): λες και περίμενε (les ke perímene = as if she was expecting).
Κι ας (ki as) is literally 'and let', and it works as 'even though': κι ας είχαν σκορπίσει (ki as íkhan skorpísi = even though they had scattered).
Έχω να (ékho na) = it has been a while since: είχε να την ακούσει (íkhe na tin akúsi = it had been long since he heard it).
Κολλάω (koláo) literally means 'stick', so κάτι δεν κόλλαγε (káti dhen kólaghe = something didn't stick) is Greek for 'something didn't add up'.
The ongoing past form covers repeated actions too: κάθε στροφή τον απομάκρυνε (káthe strofí ton apomákrine = each bend drew him further).
Μα (ma) is an everyday 'but' alongside αλλά (alá), often with a touch of emphasis: όχι με ρολόγια μα με προσευχές (ókhi me rolóyia ma me prosefkhés = not by clocks but by prayers).
Λάδι (ládhi) is literally 'oil': η θάλασσα ήταν λάδι (i thálasa ítan ládhi = the sea was oil). Where English sees glass in a calm sea, Greek sees oil.
Θα (tha) + the ongoing past form = 'would': θα έδινε τα πάντα (tha édhine ta pánda = he would give everything), a wish that stays out of reach.
Το να (to na) + verb turns an action into a thing you can talk about: το να σηκώνεσαι ξανά (to na sikónese ksaná) = getting up again.
Αφενός (afenós)... αφετέρου (afetéru) is a fixed pair, literally 'from one side... from the other': when you see αφενός, expect αφετέρου later on.
Εν κατακλείδι (en kataklídhi) = in conclusion; a frozen ancient phrase – modern Greek says σε (se), not εν (en), outside set expressions like this one.
Θα μπορούσε να υποστηριχθεί (tha borúse na ipostirikhthí = it could be argued) has no word for 'it' – Greek leaves out the dummy subject English has to supply.
Δεδομένου ότι (dhedhoménu óti) = given that. It is a frozen phrase: the -ου (-u) ending is left over from older Greek and stays the same whatever follows.
Συνεπώς (sinepós = therefore) is the lighter way to draw a conclusion; κατά συνέπεια (katá sinépia) says the same thing with more formal weight.
Ενδεχομένως (endhekhoménos = possibly) can push the main verb into the να (na) form: να μας εμποδίζει (na mas embodhízi = it may prevent us), so the doubt shows on the verb.
The comma inside ό,τι (ó,ti = whatever) is part of the word: without it, ότι (óti) means 'that'. Here ό,τι κάνει (ó,ti káni) = whatever makes.
Προκειμένου να (prokiménu na = in order to) is the report-writing twin of everyday για να (ya na): προκειμένου να διασφαλιστεί (prokiménu na dhiasfalistí) = so as to ensure.
